scope: 20 original AQA AS Chemistry mock short-recall flashcards across atomic/isotopes, ionic/covalent bonding, Group 2, inorganic precipitation/halide tests, and halogenoalkane reactions.
method: Use exact original core ID/front/back and Chemistry AS mock active guards, preserve existing accept/reject alternatives, verify original model answers plus 20 new correct and 40 incorrect responses with the live production card evaluator.
limitations: These questions remain concise recall; mechanisms and multistep calculations stay separate.
A sample of 20 calibrated responses is not independent proof of complete AQA mock specification coverage or arbitrary paraphrase accuracy.
No original card/question IDs, saved scores, XP, sign-in, sync or World content are changed.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How many electrons are in a 3+ ion formed from Z=13?
accept: An atom with atomic number 13 loses three electrons to form a 3+ ion, leaving 10 electrons.
reject: A 3+ ion of an element with Z=13 has 16 electrons.
The 3+ ion still has 13 electrons because ionisation changes the nucleus instead.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why do isotopes often have similar chemical properties?
rows.originalBack: They have the same electron arrangements despite differing neutron numbers.
accept: Neutral isotopes of an element have identical electron configurations, despite having different numbers of neutrons.
reject: Isotopes have different chemical properties mainly because they have different numbers of electrons.
Isotopes of one element must have different proton numbers.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How do you calculate Ar from two isotope abundances?
accept: Multiply each isotope mass by its abundance, add the contributions and divide by total abundance.
reject: Use the ordinary mean of isotope masses regardless of abundance.
Divide the sum of isotope masses by the atomic number without weighting.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why is Ar of an isotope mixture a weighted mean?
rows.originalBack: More abundant isotopes contribute more to the average mass.
accept: The weighted mean uses natural abundances, so the most common isotope contributes more to relative atomic mass.
reject: All isotopes contribute equally to Ar irrespective of relative abundance.
Only the heaviest isotope contributes to relative atomic mass.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: State the complete definition of ionic bonding.
rows.originalBack: Strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice.
accept: An ionic bond is a strong electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions in an ionic lattice.
reject: Ionic bonding is just a shared electron pair attracted to two nuclei.
Ionic bonds are weak London attractions between neutral molecules.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Define a single covalent bond accurately.
rows.originalBack: One electron pair shared between atoms and attracted to both nuclei.
accept: A single covalent bond is one shared pair of electrons attracted to the nuclei of both bonded atoms.
reject: A covalent bond consists of a pair of electrons completely transferred to another atom.
In a covalent bond, the electron pair is attracted to just one nucleus.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How many shared pairs are in a double and a triple covalent bond?
rows.originalBack: Two and three shared electron pairs respectively.
accept: A double bond contains two shared pairs; a triple bond contains three shared pairs.
reject: A double bond has one shared electron pair and a triple bond has two.
A double bond has three shared pairs and a triple bond has four.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is a coordinate or dative covalent bond?
rows.originalBack: A shared pair where both electrons originate from one atom.
accept: A dative covalent bond is a shared electron pair supplied by just one of the two bonded atoms.
reject: Both atoms must supply exactly one electron to a dative bond.
In a dative bond, the pair stops being shared and becomes an ionic bond.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Which species donates the lone pair in NH₃→BF₃?
rows.originalBack: The nitrogen atom in NH₃ donates to electron-deficient boron in BF₃.
accept: The lone pair on nitrogen of ammonia is donated to boron in electron-deficient BF3.
reject: Boron donates a lone pair to nitrogen in NH3.
A fluorine atom of BF3 supplies the bond pair directly to nitrogen of NH3.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How does first ionisation energy change down Group 2?
accept: The first ionisation energy decreases as you move down Group 2.
reject: First ionisation energy increases down Group 2.
First ionisation energy is identical for all Group 2 elements.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What forms when a Group 2 metal reacts with water?
accept: When a Group 2 metal reacts with water, it forms a metal hydroxide and releases hydrogen gas.
reject: Group 2 metals reacting with water form a sulfate and oxygen.
The products of Group 2 metal and water are a metal chloride and carbon dioxide.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the trend in Group 2 hydroxide solubility?
accept: Group 2 metal hydroxides generally become more soluble down the group.
reject: Group 2 hydroxide solubility falls as you go down the group.
Every Group 2 hydroxide has exactly the same solubility in water.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the trend in Group 2 sulfate solubility?
accept: Group 2 sulfate solubility decreases as you move down the group.
reject: Group 2 sulfates become more soluble down the group.
Group 2 sulfate solubility is constant across the entire group.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Write the net ionic equation for barium sulfate precipitation.
accept: The ionic precipitation equation is Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s).
reject: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(aq), which stays dissolved.
Ba²⁺(aq) + 2SO₄²⁻(aq) → Ba(SO₄)₂(s).

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What colour precipitate indicates chloride with silver ions?
accept: A white silver chloride precipitate, AgCl, identifies chloride ions with Ag+.
reject: Chloride gives a yellow AgI precipitate when silver nitrate is added.
Chloride gives a cream AgBr precipitate with silver ions.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What colour precipitate indicates bromide with silver ions?
accept: A cream precipitate of silver bromide, AgBr, indicates bromide ions.
reject: Bromide gives a white precipitate of AgCl with silver ions.
Bromide gives yellow AgI instead of cream AgBr.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What colour precipitate indicates iodide with silver ions?
accept: A yellow precipitate of silver iodide, AgI, indicates iodide ions.
reject: Iodide forms a white AgCl precipitate on adding silver ions.
Iodide gives a cream AgBr precipitate rather than yellow AgI.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What bond property makes halogenoalkanes reactive?
accept: The carbon–halogen bond is polar because halogen is more electronegative, leaving carbon partially positive.
reject: The C–halogen bond is completely non-polar.
The halogen has a partial positive charge and carbon has a partial negative charge in a halogenoalkane.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is nucleophilic substitution?
rows.originalBack: A nucleophile replaces another atom or group.
accept: In nucleophilic substitution, a nucleophile replaces a leaving atom or group.
reject: A nucleophile substitutes itself by leaving the molecule without replacement.
Nucleophilic substitution means adding across a carbon-carbon double bond with no group replaced.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What happens in elimination from a halogenoalkane?
rows.originalBack: H and a halogen leave, creating a C=C bond.
accept: Elimination removes hydrogen and halogen from a halogenoalkane to create a carbon-carbon double bond.
reject: Elimination replaces the halogen by OH to give an alcohol without forming C=C.
Halogenoalkane elimination converts the molecule to an aldehyde without loss of hydrogen or halogen.
